# Isaiah 53 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in this chapter.

In this chapter there is an important teaching or prophecy about the Messiah and his life and ministry. It begins in [52:13](../52/13.md) and scholars usually note that it portrays the Messiah as a “suffering servant.” (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/christ]])

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Atonement

This chapter prophesies about the death of Christ for sin. Most scholars believe it teaches that Christ was a righteous man who died for the sins of mankind. This is usually referred to as the atonement. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/righteous]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/atonement]])

Quote: Who has believed what they heard from us
Note: What Isaiah just found out is so amazing that he wonders if the exiles will believe it. The “we” includes him and those in exile. Alternate translation: [It is hard for anyone to believe what we have heard] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

Quote: to whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?
Note: Arm refers to God’s power. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has revealed his power to people.] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

Quote: For he grew up before Yahweh like a sapling
Note: Here “he” refers to God’s servant whom Isaiah compares to a very young tree. This emphasizes that he will appear weak.
“parched earth” is hard and dry ground that will not allow plants to grow and represents where the servant of Yahweh will come. Alternate translation: [out of an impossible situation]

Quote: He was despised and rejected by people
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People considered him as nothing and rejected him]
Alternate translation: [a man knowing all kinds of sadness]

Quote: from whom men hide their faces
Note: “Face” represents a person’s attention or fellowship. Hiding one’s face means to turn away from someone. Alternate translation: [from whom people turn away]

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they considered him to be worthless]

Quote: he has borne our sicknesses and carried our sorrows
Note: To “bear” or carry an abstraction like sickness and sorrow represents taking it up. Alternate translation: [he has taken our sicknesses and sorrows upon himself]

Quote: yet we thought he was being punished by God, struck by God, and afflicted
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [yet we thought God was punishing and afflicting him] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

Quote: But he was pierced because of our rebellious deeds; he was crushed because of our sins
Note: These two phrases share similar meanings and emphasize that the servant suffered because of the people’s sins. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God allowed the enemy to stab him and kill him because of our sins] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

Quote: The punishment for our peace was on him
Note: This refers to peace with God. This can be made explicit. Alternate translation: [He accepted this punishment so we could live in harmony]

Quote: with his wounds we are healed
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he healed us by his suffering of the wounds]

Quote: We all like sheep have gone astray
Note: Sheep often leave the path on which the shepherd leads them. Isaiah means that we do what we want instead of what God commands.
Our “iniquity” here represents the guilt for our sin. Alternate translation: [the guilt for the sin of every one of us]
If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They treated him harshly]

Quote: he did not open his mouth
Note: “Mouth” represents what a person says. Opening one’s mouth means to speak. Alternate translation: [he did not protest]

Quote: as a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent
Note: Isaiah compares the servant to a lamb and a sheep to emphasize that he will remain silent as people harm and humiliate him.

Quote: as a lamb that is led to the slaughter
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [just as a lamb is silent as a person slaughters it] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They treated him harshly, judged him, and condemned him]

Note: This question emphasizes that no one thinks about him. Alternate translation: [no one from his generation cared what happened to him.] or [no one among his contemporaries cared what happened to him.]

Note: Many versions interpret this passage in Hebrew differently: “Who can say anything about his descendants?” or “Who can say anything about his fate?”

Note: “Cut off” here refers to death. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Note: “Mouth” represents what a person says. Alternate translation: [nor did he deceive anyone when he spoke]

# Isaiah 54 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in this chapter.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness

This chapter focuses on Yahweh’s faithfulness to fulfill his covenants. It references several different covenant promises in this chapter. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenantfaith]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/faithful]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/fulfill]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]])

Quote: you barren woman … children of the married woman
Note: Yahweh telling the people of Jerusalem to rejoice because there will be many people living in Jerusalem again is spoken of as if Yahweh were telling a barren women she is going to have many children.

Quote: break into joyful singing and cry aloud, you who have never been in birth labor
Note: This statement means the same thing as the first part of the sentence.

Here “you” is singular and refers to the barren woman. She represents herself and all of her descendants. Alternate translation: [For you and your descendants will spread out] (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])
Here “nations” represents the people. Alternate translation: [will conquer the people of other nations]

Quote: For your Maker is your husband
Note: Yahweh loving and taking care of his people is spoken of as if he were their husband.

See how you translated this in [Isaiah 1:24](../01/24.md).
See how you translated this in [Isaiah 5:16](../05/16.md).
See how you translated this in [Isaiah 41:14](../41/14.md).

Quote: he is called the God of the whole earth
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he is the God of the whole earth]

Quote: Yahweh has called you back as a wife … like a woman married young and rejected
Note: Yahweh sending his people away into exile then bringing them back is spoken of as if Yahweh were a husband who had rejected his wife but now accepts her. (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

Note: Yahweh continuing to love his people is spoken of as if his love would not turn away from the people. Alternate translation: [I will not stop loving you]

## Structure and Formatting

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Fasting

The practice of fasting became more common after the exile. This was intended to bring people into a right relationship with God by creating a designated time to concentrate on him. It may have been believed that Yahweh heard people better when they fasted. The significance of fasting is derived from the faster’s attitude of repentance and faith in Yahweh and not the practice itself. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/repent]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/faith]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “Yet they seek me daily”

The people did not truly seek Yahweh every day. They practiced the outward aspects of the Jewish religion, but their hearts were far from Yahweh. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

Quote: Lift up your voice like a trumpet
Note: This means shout loudly. Here “your” refers to Isaiah. (See also: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-you]])

Note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. Together they strengthen the urgency to confront Yahweh’s people.

Quote: ‘Why have we fasted,’ they say, ‘but you do not see it? Why have we humbled ourselves, but you do not notice?’
Note: The people of Israel use questions to complain to God because they feel he is ignoring them.
“Behold!” or “Pay attention.” Yahweh confronts their questioning by telling them to pay attention.
“wicked fist.” This shows that they fight viciously. “Fist” represents anger that is physically violent.

# Isaiah 66 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 66:1–17, 21–24.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### In the end

In the end, Yahweh will enact his perfect justice. This is the true hope of this world. The new heaven and the new earth are an important part of this. In the end, this will be the perfect creation of Yahweh and will last forever. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/hope]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/eternity]])

Note: Yahweh compares heaven to a throne and the earth to a footstool to emphasize how great he is.

Note: Yahweh uses questions to emphasize that humans cannot build a place for him to dwell.
